question: What is emergency contraception
answer: Emergency contraception (EC) is birth control used after unprotected sex to prevent pregnancy. It's not an abortion pill and won't end an existing pregnancy. Options include: 1) Levonorgestrel pills (Plan B One-Step, Take Action) - over-the-counter, effective up to 72 hours after sex (can work up to 5 days but less effective). 2) Ulipristal acetate (Ella) - prescription, effective up to 5 days. 3) Copper IUD - most effective, can be inserted up to 5 days after sex and provides ongoing contraception. EC works primarily by delaying ovulation.

question: How does emergency contraception work
alternate_questions: How does morning after pill work
answer: Emergency contraception works primarily by delaying or preventing ovulation. If ovulation has already occurred, EC is unlikely to be effective because it doesn't interfere with fertilization or implantation of an already fertilized egg. Levonorgestrel (Plan B) is a high dose of the same hormone in regular birth control pills. Ulipristal acetate (Ella) is a progesterone receptor modulator that delays ovulation more effectively than levonorgestrel, especially closer to ovulation. The copper IUD works by creating a toxic environment for sperm, preventing fertilization. EC is not an abortifacient.

question: How effective is Plan B
alternate_questions: How well does Plan B work
answer: Plan B (levonorgestrel) reduces the risk of pregnancy by about 75-89% when taken within 72 hours of unprotected sex. It's most effective the sooner you take it - within 24 hours is best. Effectiveness decreases over time: about 95% effective within 24 hours, 85% within 48 hours, and 58% within 72 hours. It may still work up to 5 days after sex but with significantly reduced effectiveness. Effectiveness is lower in women with higher BMI (over 165 lbs or 75 kg). Plan B does not work if ovulation has already occurred. It is less effective than regular contraception methods.

question: How effective is Ella
answer: Ella (ulipristal acetate) is effective up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sex and maintains its effectiveness throughout that window, unlike Plan B which decreases over time. It reduces pregnancy risk by about 85% overall. Ella is more effective than Plan B, especially between days 3-5 after sex and for women with higher BMI. It works by blocking progesterone receptors to delay ovulation more effectively than levonorgestrel, even when taken close to ovulation. Ella requires a prescription in most countries. It is not recommended if you are already taking hormonal contraception.

question: How effective is copper IUD for emergency contraception
answer: The copper IUD (Paragard) is the most effective form of emergency contraception, preventing over 99% of pregnancies when inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex. Unlike pills, it works even if ovulation has already occurred by creating a toxic environment for sperm and preventing fertilization. It can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sex or up to 5 days after estimated ovulation. The major advantage is that it provides ongoing contraception for up to 10-12 years after insertion. It requires a healthcare provider for insertion. Side effects may include heavier periods and cramping initially.

question: Emergency contraception side effects
alternate_questions: What to expect after emergency contraception
answer: Common side effects of emergency contraception include: nausea (sometimes with vomiting), fatigue, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, and changes to your next period (earlier, later, heavier, lighter, or spotting). These usually resolve within a few days. If you vomit within 2-3 hours of taking EC, you may need another dose. Your next period may be delayed by up to a week. If your period is more than 1 week late, take a pregnancy test. Serious side effects are rare. EC does not affect long-term fertility. If you experience severe abdominal pain, seek medical care as this could indicate an ectopic pregnancy.

answer: No, emergency contraception is not an abortion pill and does not terminate an existing pregnancy. EC works primarily by delaying or preventing ovulation. question: Can I take emergency contraception during my period
answer: Yes, you can take emergency contraception during your period. EC is safe to take at any point in your cycle, though it is most urgently needed if taken close to ovulation.

question: Does breastfeeding affect emergency contraception
answer: Levonorgestrel (Plan B) is considered safe during breastfeeding. Small amounts may pass into breast milk but are not harmful to the baby. You do not need to pump and dump. Ulipristal acetate (Ella) is generally not recommended during breastfeeding because it may affect milk supply and its effects on infants are less studied; if used, pump and discard milk for 24 hours. The copper IUD is safe during breastfeeding and does not affect milk supply. Progestin-only pills are also safe while breastfeeding. If you are exclusively breastfeeding and your baby is under 6 months old, you may have some natural contraceptive protection (lactational amenorrhea method), though this is not 100% effective.

question: Emergency contraception and drug interactions
answer: Certain medications can reduce emergency contraception effectiveness. These include: enzyme-inducing drugs like rifampin (antibiotic for TB), some anti-seizure medications (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, oxcarbazepine), some HIV medications, and St. John's Wort herbal supplement. These drugs speed up liver metabolism of hormones. Most common antibiotics do NOT affect EC. If you take these medications, the copper IUD is the best EC option as it is not affected by drug interactions. If using oral EC, you may need a higher dose or alternative - consult a healthcare provider. Ella may have more interactions than Plan B due to its mechanism.

question: What is the difference between emergency contraception and abortion pill
answer: Emergency contraception and the abortion pill are completely different medications with different purposes. Emergency contraception (Plan B, Ella) prevents pregnancy BEFORE it starts by delaying ovulation. It will not work if you are already pregnant and will not harm an existing pregnancy. The abortion pill (mifepristone and misoprostol) terminates an EXISTING pregnancy up to 10 weeks gestation. EC is taken within 5 days of unprotected sex. The abortion pill is taken after pregnancy is confirmed. EC is available over-the-counter in many places; the abortion pill requires a prescription and medical supervision. EC prevents fertilization or implantation; the abortion pill causes uterine contractions to expel an established pregnancy. They are not interchangeable.

question: Does emergency contraception protect against STIs
answer: No, emergency contraception does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, herpes, or HPV. EC only prevents pregnancy. If you had unprotected sex and are concerned about STIs, consider getting tested. Many STIs have no symptoms but can cause serious health problems if untreated. Condoms are the only contraceptive method that also protects against STIs. If there was a risk of HIV exposure (unprotected sex with someone who is HIV positive or of unknown status), consider post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours. Contact a healthcare provider or sexual health clinic for STI testing and PEP if indicated.

question: What is the Yuzpe method
answer: The Yuzpe method is an older emergency contraception technique using regular combined oral contraceptive pills (those containing both estrogen and progestin) taken in specific doses within 72 hours of unprotected sex. It involves taking a certain number of birth control pills, then repeating the dose 12 hours later. It is less effective than dedicated EC pills and causes more nausea due to higher estrogen doses. The Yuzpe method is generally not recommended anymore because dedicated EC (Plan B, Ella) is more effective, better tolerated, and widely available. However, it may be useful in situations where dedicated EC is unavailable. Not all birth control pills can be used for the Yuzpe method - specific formulations are required. question: Is there emergency contraception for men

question: Can I swim after taking emergency contraception
answer: Yes, you can swim, exercise, shower, bathe, and engage in all normal activities after taking emergency contraception. There are no activity restrictions after taking EC pills. Water and physical activity do not affect the medication's absorption or effectiveness. You can resume your normal routine immediately. The only consideration is if you experience nausea or vomiting after taking EC - avoid strenuous activity if you feel nauseated, and seek a second dose if you vomit within 2-3 hours. After copper IUD insertion for emergency contraception, your provider may advise avoiding swimming or baths for 24-48 hours to reduce infection risk, but showers are fine. Otherwise, live your life normally.

question: Does emergency contraception cause weight gain
answer: Emergency contraception does not cause long-term weight gain. You may experience temporary bloating or mild water retention for a few days after taking EC due to the hormone dose, but this resolves quickly. EC does not cause fat gain or permanent body composition changes. Some people may feel their clothes fit tighter for 2-3 days due to bloating. If you experience significant or persistent weight gain, it is due to other factors (diet, activity, other medications, underlying conditions) not EC. If you are concerned about weight, focus on regular exercise and balanced nutrition. For ongoing contraception, some methods like the shot (Depo-Provera) may be associated with weight gain in some users, but EC pills do not have this effect.

question: Can I take emergency contraception if I have PCOS
answer: Yes, emergency contraception is safe to take if you have PCOS. EC works the same way in people with PCOS as in those without. However, PCOS can cause irregular ovulation, making it harder to predict your fertile window. This means you might need EC at unexpected times. EC is effective for people with PCOS, though if you have a higher BMI associated with PCOS, Plan B may be less effective - Ella or copper IUD would be better options. EC does not worsen PCOS symptoms long-term, though it may temporarily worsen cycle irregularity. If you have PCOS and are not trying to conceive, consider a regular contraception method that also helps manage PCOS symptoms, such as combined hormonal contraception which regulates cycles and reduces androgen symptoms.

question: Can I take emergency contraception with endometriosis
answer: Yes, emergency contraception is safe to take if you have endometriosis. EC does not worsen endometriosis or cause endometriosis flares. The hormone dose in EC is short-term and does not significantly affect endometrial tissue. However, EC may cause temporary menstrual irregularities which could be uncomfortable if you already have painful periods. If you have endometriosis and are not trying to conceive, consider regular contraception that also helps manage endometriosis symptoms. Continuous combined hormonal contraception (skipping placebo weeks) or progestin-only methods can suppress endometriosis growth and reduce pain. The copper IUD is generally not recommended for endometriosis as it may worsen bleeding and cramps. Discuss long-term options with your gynecologist.

question: Emergency contraception and ectopic pregnancy
answer: Emergency contraception does not increase the risk of ectopic pregnancy. However, EC is less effective at preventing ectopic pregnancy than uterine pregnancy, so if EC fails, there is a slightly higher chance the pregnancy could be ectopic compared to a natural conception. This is a small absolute risk. If you take EC and experience severe abdominal pain (especially one-sided), shoulder pain, dizziness, fainting, or vaginal bleeding with pain, seek emergency medical care immediately as these are signs of possible ectopic pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is life-threatening and requires immediate treatment. EC does not cause ectopic pregnancy - it simply may be less effective at preventing implantation outside the uterus. Regular contraception is more effective at preventing all pregnancies including ectopic.

question: Can I take emergency contraception with an IUD
answer: If you already have a copper IUD, you do not need emergency contraception - the copper IUD itself is the most effective EC method and provides ongoing protection. If you have a hormonal IUD (Mirena, Kyleena, Liletta, Skyla) and are concerned about pregnancy due to late insertion, partial expulsion, or other issues, EC is generally not needed as hormonal IUDs are highly effective. However, if your hormonal IUD was inserted more than 7 days ago and you had unprotected sex without backup, or if you suspect expulsion, consult your provider. If you need EC and want an IUD, the copper IUD can be inserted for EC even if you previously had a hormonal IUD removed. Do not use Ella if you have a hormonal IUD in place.

question: What is the most effective emergency contraception
alternate_questions: Best option prevent pregnancy after sex
answer: The copper IUD (Paragard) is the most effective emergency contraception, preventing over 99% of pregnancies when inserted within 5 days of unprotected sex. It works even if ovulation has already occurred, unlike pills. It also provides ongoing contraception for 10-12 years. Among pills, Ella (ulipristal) is more effective than Plan B (levonorgestrel), especially on days 3-5 and for women with higher BMI. Effectiveness ranking: 1) Copper IUD (>99% effective), 2) Ella (85% effective up to 5 days), 3) Plan B (75-89% effective within 72 hours, decreasing over time). The best choice depends on timing, access, cost, and whether you want ongoing contraception. If you can access a copper IUD within 5 days, it is the superior choice.

question: Does emergency contraception work if I am ovulating
answer: Emergency contraception pills work primarily by delaying ovulation. If you have already ovulated (the egg has been released), EC pills are unlikely to prevent pregnancy because they do not interfere with fertilization or implantation of a fertilized egg. However, it can be difficult to know exactly when ovulation occurs, so taking EC is still recommended if you had unprotected sex. Ella (ulipristal) may have some effect closer to ovulation than Plan B because it blocks progesterone receptors more effectively. The copper IUD is the only EC method that works after ovulation because it creates a toxic environment for sperm and prevents fertilization. If you track ovulation and know you ovulated before sex, the copper IUD is your best option if within 5 days.

question: Can I take emergency contraception after ovulation
alternate_questions: Can EC work after egg release
answer: If ovulation has definitely already occurred and the egg has been released, emergency contraception pills (Plan B, Ella) are unlikely to work because they primarily prevent ovulation, not fertilization or implantation. However, sperm can survive up to 5 days, so if you had sex before ovulation but ovulated shortly after, EC taken immediately after sex may still prevent ovulation. The copper IUD is the only EC option that works after ovulation because it prevents fertilization by creating a sperm-toxic environment. If you are past ovulation and within 5 days of sex, the copper IUD is your only effective EC option. If you are beyond 5 days after sex, no EC will work - wait for your period and take a pregnancy test if late.

question: Does emergency contraception work during fertile window
answer: Emergency contraception can work during your fertile window, but effectiveness varies. EC pills are most effective when taken BEFORE ovulation occurs, as they delay the release of the egg. If taken during the fertile window but before ovulation, EC can still prevent pregnancy by postponing ovulation. If taken on the day of ovulation or after, pills are much less effective. The copper IUD works throughout the entire fertile window and even after ovulation because it prevents sperm from reaching the egg. If you know you are in your fertile window, take EC as soon as possible - every hour matters. Ella is more effective than Plan B during the fertile window, especially close to ovulation. The copper IUD is the best option if you can access it within 5 days.

question: Can I take emergency contraception with the implant
answer: If you have a contraceptive implant (Nexplanon/Implanon) that was inserted correctly and within its effective period (3-5 years), you typically do not need emergency contraception as the implant is over 99% effective. However, if your implant was inserted less than 7 days ago and you had unprotected sex during that time, or if you suspect the implant has moved, broken, or is overdue for replacement, you may need backup. If you need EC while having an implant, Plan B is safe to use. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) with a hormonal implant as it can reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is also an option. If you are concerned about implant failure, check that you can feel the implant under your skin and consult your provider.

question: Emergency contraception and the birth control shot
alternate_questions: Morning after pill while on shot
answer: If you are up-to-date on your Depo-Provera shots (every 12-13 weeks) and received them on time, you typically do not need emergency contraception as the shot is over 99% effective when used correctly. However, if your shot was late (more than 2 weeks overdue), you may need backup contraception or EC if you had unprotected sex. If you need EC while on Depo, Plan B is safe to use. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) if you are on Depo-Provera or have used it in the past 14 days, as the progestin in Depo can reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is a good alternative if you need EC and are on Depo. If your shot was late, use backup contraception for 7 days after getting back on schedule.

question: Can I take emergency contraception with the patch
answer: If you use the contraceptive patch correctly and consistently, you typically do not need emergency contraception. However, you may need EC if your patch fell off for more than 24 hours, was applied late after the patch-free week, or if you had unprotected sex during the first week of patch use without backup. If you need EC while using the patch, Plan B is safe. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) if you are currently using the patch, as the hormones can interact and reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is an alternative. After taking Plan B, continue your patch schedule but use backup contraception (condoms) for 7 days. If your patch fell off, replace it and use backup for 7 days.

question: Emergency contraception and the vaginal ring
answer: If you use the vaginal ring correctly, you typically do not need emergency contraception. You may need EC if your ring was out for more than 3 hours (NuvaRing) or more than 2 hours (Annovera), if you left it in past the recommended time, or if you had unprotected sex during the first week without backup. If you need EC while using the ring, Plan B is safe. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) if you are currently using a hormonal vaginal ring, as the hormones can reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is an alternative. After taking Plan B, reinsert or replace your ring and use backup contraception for 7 days. If the ring was out too long, you may need to start a new cycle.

question: Can I take emergency contraception with mini pill
alternate_questions: Plan B with progestin only pill
answer: If you take the progestin-only pill (mini pill) correctly every day at the same time, you typically do not need emergency contraception. However, if you are more than 3 hours late taking a traditional norethindrone mini pill (or more than 24 hours late for drospirenone mini pills like Slynd), you may need backup contraception or EC if you had unprotected sex. If you need EC while on the mini pill, Plan B is safe to use. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) if you are on progestin-only pills, as the progestin can reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is an alternative. After taking Plan B, continue your mini pill but use backup contraception for 2 days (traditional mini pill) or 7 days (drospirenone).

question: Emergency contraception and combined birth control pills
alternate_questions: Morning after pill combined oral contraceptive
answer: If you take combined birth control pills correctly, you typically do not need emergency contraception. You may need EC if you missed 2 or more active pills in a row (days 1-2 of pack or days 15-21), had vomiting or severe diarrhea within 2 hours of taking pills, or took interacting medications. If you need EC while on combined pills, Plan B is safe. Do not use Ella (ulipristal) if you are currently on combined hormonal contraception or have used it in the past 5 days, as it can reduce Ella's effectiveness. The copper IUD is an alternative. After taking Plan B, continue your regular pills and use backup contraception for 7 days. If you missed pills, follow your pill's specific instructions for missed doses.

question: What is the window for copper IUD emergency contraception
alternate_questions: How late can I get copper IUD after sex
answer: The copper IUD can be inserted up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sex for emergency contraception. It can also be inserted up to 5 days after estimated ovulation, which may extend the window if ovulation occurred late. This is the longest effective window of any EC method, and unlike pills, the copper IUD maintains its effectiveness throughout the entire 5-day period. It is over 99% effective at preventing pregnancy and provides ongoing contraception for 10-12 years. If you are approaching the 5-day deadline, contact a provider immediately. Some clinics offer same-day or next-day insertion appointments. The IUD must be inserted by a trained healthcare provider.

question: Does emergency contraception affect my next ovulation
answer: Emergency contraception can delay your next ovulation by a few days to a week, which is why your next period may be late. This delay is temporary and does not affect long-term fertility or future cycles. Your ovulation should return to normal in the following cycle. EC does not 'reset' your cycle permanently. If you use EC frequently, you may experience more irregular ovulation timing. If your period is more than 1 week late after taking EC, take a pregnancy test. After taking EC, use backup contraception until your next period because ovulation timing may be unpredictable. Tracking your cycle with an app can help you understand when ovulation returns to normal.

question: Can I take emergency contraception if I have migraines
answer: Yes, emergency contraception is generally safe for people with migraines. Unlike combined hormonal contraception, which is contraindicated in people with migraine with aura due to stroke risk, EC contains only progestin (Plan B) or ulipristal (Ella) - neither of which carries the same stroke risk as estrogen. If you have migraine with aura, you can safely use Plan B or Ella. The copper IUD is also completely safe and hormone-free. Some people may experience a temporary headache after taking EC, but this is not dangerous and usually resolves within 24 hours. If you experience a severe headache after EC that is different from your usual migraines, or if you have neurological symptoms (vision changes, weakness, confusion), seek medical care.

question: Emergency contraception and blood clot risk
answer: Emergency contraception does not significantly increase blood clot risk. Unlike combined hormonal contraception which contains estrogen and carries a small increased risk of blood clots, EC pills (Plan B and Ella) do not contain estrogen. Plan B contains levonorgestrel (progestin only), and Ella contains ulipristal acetate. Neither has been associated with increased thrombosis risk. The copper IUD is completely hormone-free and has no clotting risk. If you have a history of blood clots, stroke, or are at high risk for thrombosis, EC is still safe for you. However, if you are looking for ongoing contraception, avoid combined hormonal methods and consider progestin-only or non-hormonal options. Always inform your provider of your clotting history.
